content: In 2017, the World Health Organization (WHO) published a document outlining the terms under which its work could be used, emphasizing that the material could be copied, redistributed, and adapted for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation was given. However, the use of the WHO logo was prohibited, and any adaptations of the work required licensing under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. Translations of the work needed to include a disclaimer stating that WHO was not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation, with the original English version remaining the authoritative edition. The publication, titled Medication Without Harm: Global Patient Safety Challenge on Medication Safety, highlighted the importance of addressing unsafe medication practices and errors, which are a leading cause of avoidable harm in healthcare systems worldwide. The WHO Patient Safety Programme, established over a decade ago, has raised global awareness about patient safety concepts and strategies, secured commitments from health ministers and leaders, and provided evidence-based guidance and tools to improve patient safety. The program has also emphasized the importance of learning from the experiences of patients and families affected by unsafe care. The WHO has launched two Global Patient Safety Challenges in the past and, based on feedback from stakeholders and experts, initiated a third challenge focused on medication safety. This challenge aims to reduce severe, avoidable medication-related harm by 50% globally over five years. It seeks to address weaknesses in healthcare systems and improve practices at all stages of the medication process, including prescribing, dispensing, administration, and monitoring. Unsafe medication practices and errors are significant contributors to patient harm, with the global cost of medication errors estimated at $42 billion annually. Patients in low-income countries experience twice as many disability-adjusted life years lost due to medication-related harm compared to those in high-income countries. Errors often occur due to weak medication systems and human factors such as fatigue, poor working conditions, or staff shortages. These errors can result in severe harm, disability, or death, with administration errors being the most frequent, though risks exist at all stages of the medication process. The third Global Patient Safety Challenge emphasizes the need for systemic improvements to reduce medication errors and harm. It focuses on high-risk situations, polypharmacy (the use of multiple medications), and transitions of care, which are particularly vulnerable to errors. The challenge also highlights the importance of empowering patients and the public to play an active role in their medication safety, improving healthcare professionals' practices, and addressing the complexity and dysfunction of medication systems. Key objectives of the challenge include assessing the scope of avoidable harm, creating actionable frameworks for improvement, developing tools and technologies to support safer medication use, engaging stakeholders to raise awareness, and empowering patients to manage their medications safely. The challenge also emphasizes the need for political leadership and national-level commitment to prioritize medication safety. It will also promote research, engage with regulatory agencies, and involve patients and families in all aspects of the challenge. Collaboration with ministries of health, healthcare leaders, educational institutions, regulatory authorities, patient advocacy groups, and the pharmaceutical industry will be essential to achieving the challenge's goals. The document also shares a personal story of a young woman named Martha, who tragically died due to a series of medical errors and an adverse medication reaction. Her death highlights the critical need for transparency, reporting, and systemic changes to prevent similar tragedies. The story serves as a call to action to improve medication safety and honor those who have been harmed by unsafe care. In summary, the third Global Patient Safety Challenge on Medication Safety aims to reduce medication-related harm through systemic improvements, stakeholder engagement, and patient empowerment. By addressing high-risk situations, polypharmacy, and care transitions, the challenge seeks to create safer healthcare systems and improve outcomes for patients worldwide.
